Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +1).
$$

Letting $\theta =\frac{x}{4},$ we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{x}{4})=\frac{1}{2}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})+1].
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int [{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{x}{4})-1]\text{d}x & =\int [\frac{1}{2}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})+1]-1]\text{d}x \\  & =\int [\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})+\frac{1}{2}-1]\text{d}x \\  & =\int [\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})-\frac{1}{2}]\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})]-\frac{1}{2}x+C \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})-\frac{x}{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$
